claims.text: Successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by a balance between interacting-element kinetic energy and alloy-phase thermodynamic stability.
The relevant initial material is a multimetal nanoparticle system containing more than five interacting elements.
Controlled variation of synthesis conditions can modulate the kinetic energy of the interacting elements.
The proposed synthesis requires a high-temperature environment with precise control of reaction kinetics.
Alloy-phase stability is the structural mediator of successful nanoparticle formation.
Kinetic control of element interactions determines whether homogeneous alloy formation or phase separation occurs.
Controlled synthesis conditions will improve formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles relative to an unchanged baseline.
The resulting nanoparticles will retain substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications.
The baseline is characterized by uncontrolled morphology.
The baseline is characterized by high decomposition temperatures.
The hypothesis applies to multimetal nanoparticle systems containing more than five interacting elements.
The hypothesis may not apply to systems with fewer elements or under different synthesis conditions.
The exact relationship between interacting-element kinetic energy and alloy-phase thermodynamic stability is not well understood.
